nameStory: The word 'yew' comes from the Old English 'iw' and Germanic roots meaning 'reddish-brown,' likely referring to the tree's distinctive red-brown bark. This ancient name has stuck for thousands of years, showing just how long humans have known and valued these remarkable evergreens. The 'common' part simply means this is the most widespread yew species across Europe and much of the world.
description: Common yew is a slow-growing evergreen shrub or small tree that can live for centuries, sometimes reaching 20-30 feet tall in New England. It has a dense, spreading shape with dark green needle-like leaves arranged in flat sprays along the branches. The bark is thin and reddish-brown, often peeling in papery strips. What makes yews really special are their bright red berries (technically called arils) that appear on female plants in late summer and fall.

idTips.label: Needles
idTips.description: Flat, dark green needles about half an inch long, arranged in two rows along the stem like a feather. Feel soft and flexible, not sharp or prickly like spruce needles. The undersides are slightly paler green.

idTips.label: Red berries
idTips.description: Bright red, cup-shaped berries about the size of a small pea, appearing only on female trees. The red part is sweet and edible, but the hard seed inside is deadly poisonous.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Thin, reddish-brown to purplish bark that peels off in small, papery flakes. On older trees, it becomes more scaly and darker. Feel smooth when freshly exposed.

idTips.label: Growth form
idTips.description: Dense, bushy growth with branches that spread horizontally. Often wider than it is tall when grown in the open. Branches feel sturdy and don't droop like hemlock.

idTips.label: Branch pattern
idTips.description: Small twigs stay green for 2-3 years before turning brown. Buds are tiny and barely noticeable, covered with small overlapping scales.

habitat: In New England, common yew is mostly found in old cemeteries, historic gardens, and around colonial-era buildings where it was planted centuries ago. It occasionally escapes cultivation and grows wild in rich, moist soils along woodland edges and shaded areas. Look for it in well-drained spots that don't get waterlogged, often in the understory of mixed hardwood forests.

seasonality.spring: New bright green growth appears at branch tips, creating a two-toned effect with the darker older needles. This is when you can most easily spot the fresh growth.
seasonality.summer: Foliage is uniformly dark green and dense. Female trees may show tiny, inconspicuous flowers that will become berries later.
seasonality.fall: Bright red berries appear on female trees, creating a striking contrast with the dark green needles. This is the best time to positively identify yews.
seasonality.winter: Stays fully evergreen with dark foliage that may bronze slightly in harsh cold. Red berries often persist into early winter, providing food for birds.

funFact: Yew wood is so elastic and strong that English longbows made from yew could shoot arrows over 400 yards and pierce medieval armor – some yew longbows recovered from shipwrecks are still flexible after 500 years underwater!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Canada hemlock, but yew needles are much longer, flatter, and arranged in obvious flat sprays, while hemlock needles are tiny and short. Memory trick: 'Yew needles are Yearning to be longer' – they're noticeably bigger than hemlock's tiny needles.
contextualKnowledge: Almost every part of the yew except the red berry flesh contains taxine alkaloids that are extremely poisonous to humans and livestock – even clippings in compost can be dangerous. Despite this, yews have been planted around churches and homes for over a thousand years, symbolizing immortality due to their incredible longevity.
compareHints: Common yew has longer needles and grows taller than Canada yew, which stays low and shrubby (usually under 4 feet). Japanese yew, more common in landscaping, has needles that curve upward and inward, while common yew needles lay flat. Common yew also tends to have a more open, less dense appearance than the tightly packed Japanese yew.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canada yew is much smaller and ground-hugging compared to its relatives - common yew and Japanese yew can grow into large shrubs or small trees up to 20 feet tall.
Japanese yew grows much larger and more upright than its native cousin, Canada yew, which rarely gets taller than 3 feet and spreads along the ground.
